name: charles-accent-heroes
description: "Generate award-level landing-page hero graphics: one striking subject big enough to leave the frame, under a named light, on a textured field; big type tied to the subject; a quiet real-site interface; and one bold accent colour far around the wheel from the other two. Each page is a close variation of a reference screenshot (or a written layout), rendered with GPT Image, checked, and fixed with targeted edits. Use when someone wants a website hero image, a landing-page or hero-section mockup, poster-like site graphics, or Awwwards-style hero art for a real or fictional business."
---

# Accent heroes

Images of a website's first screen that look like award-winning posters: one striking subject on a bold field, big type tied to the subject, a quiet but real interface, and one accent colour that makes the page pop. They are pictures of websites, not code: the image model composes type, subject and light in one pass, which is what lets a headline sit behind a face or catch an object's glow.

Read [references/craft.md](references/craft.md) before writing pages. It has the decision trees for type, headline and layout, the colour formula, and the tells that make a hero look generated.

## The bar

Every page passes all eight. Each one exists because breaking it made real pages look generated or forgettable.

1. **A real business, clear in a second.** A stranger names the offer from the picture, the wordmark and the button. The nav and button use the trade's own words (Retreats, Book a retreat). A clever metaphor that hides the business fails: nobody can tell what the page is for.
2. **One poster subject, big enough to leave the frame.** One product, object or person. Either the frame crops it, or one long part of it (silk, a ribbon, a cable, light rays, glass tubes, a splash, petals) sweeps across the frame and off an edge. A whole product floating in the middle with a margin all round reads as a catalogue shot. Movement is welcome when it is shot as a poster: one dancer mid-leap or one kayaker mid-stroke, filling the frame on a plain field or a stage. Never a small figure in a wide scene: tiny faces, hands and crowds are where image models give themselves away.
3. **One bold accent.** The most vivid colour on the page, 120-180° around the wheel from the other two colours (75° at the very least), covering 15-30% of the frame. It is the subject's own main colour (its light, paint or material) and may spill onto the headline. Choose a cobalt parasol, not a cobalt-and-white one: a two-colour subject halves the accent. Never a thin line or a small object, because a polite accent leaves the page flat. When pushing the share further would add a tell, stop: a page that reads bold at 320 px beats a higher number. The one exception to the distance is the tonal route: the accent is the light itself, in the field's own colour family but far brighter than anything else (craft.md).
4. **A headline tied to the subject.** The subject lights, fills or crosses the type, or one word takes the subject's accent (craft.md's tree). A headline with no link to the picture reads as pasted on.
5. **Type that runs behind the subject, evenly spaced.** Set the headline as if the subject stepped in front of it afterwards: with the subject removed, the words would sit perfectly spaced. Never open a gap in a word to make room for the subject; it reads as type that stops for a head. The subject may hide one letter of a word that can still be read (the middle V of VIVID), never more.
6. **A material, not a flat colour.** The field is plaster, paper, ink, glass, metal or fabric from the brand's world. Flat digital colour is the first thing that looks generated.
7. **Photographed, not rendered, under a named light.** Every page names one of craft.md's light setups. Light the model isn't told about comes out soft and even, the catalogue look of the flattest pages. People get real skin and film grain. Objects keep real proportions and crisp small parts. No fire, lava or lightning unless it is the product.
8. **Three small captions at most**, each real information: a date, a spec, a price, a place. Slogans in every corner are filler.

Never use a real brand's name, logo or product, or a real person.

## References

Each page is a close variation of one reference: a screenshot of a hero section you admire, from the user's own folder of them (Awwwards, Godly and Land-book are good sources). Ask for that folder first. The reference rides along as the image the model edits, so its layout, type system, small type and finish carry over, which a written prompt alone loses. The page replaces the brand, the subject and every word.

- Crop each reference to the hero only, at 3:2, cutting away any strip of neighbouring images, and keep the crops in `<folder>/out/refs/`. Use poster-like heroes; skip SaaS heroes with logo rows and UI cards, which turn into template-looking pages.
- Never copy a reference's people, logos or text, and never publish or commit the screenshots: they are other designers' work.
- No references? Leave `ref` out. The page's `layout` then becomes a written composition. It works, but expect more re-rolls.

## Run it

Needs Python 3 with numpy, requests and Pillow, and `OPENAI_API_KEY` in the environment or in a `.env` in or above the project folder. The word check uses macOS Vision; on other systems it is skipped, so read every word by eye.

```bash
python3 -I <skill>/scripts/heroes.py <check|render|fix|review|board> --project <folder>
```

`<folder>` holds `concepts.json`. Everything generated goes to `<folder>/out/`; keep `out/` out of version control.

### 1. Plan the batch

Ask how many pages (four if unsaid) and for which businesses; invent fictional ones when none are given. Then set the batch:

- Several businesses: each a different kind (product, hospitality, studio, property, hardware, food, culture, gallery show). One business: each page a different reference and subject.
- Each reference once.
- At most half the pages share a layout; six pages or more use at least four layouts (craft.md).
- Accents spread round the wheel: no 30° stretch holds more than two.
- Adding to pages you already have? Pass their `concepts.json` with `check --also` to see which of them each new accent sits near.

### 2. Write the pages

One entry per page in `concepts.json`, keyed by a short page name:

| Field | What goes in it |
| --- | --- |
| `ref` | The reference screenshot: an absolute path, or relative to the project folder |
| `brand`, `what` | The fictional name; what it sells and to whom |
| `layout` | One of craft.md's layouts |
| `subject` | The poster subject in one sentence, its materials and light named |
| `background` | The field's material (bar 6) |
| `light` | One of craft.md's light setups by name, and where it falls: "one stage spot from high left, the dancer lit, the stage falling to dark" |
| `headline` | Two to four words: a plain promise, a name or a place. Never an idiom pun |
| `headline_note` | The type system (craft.md's tree), which word takes the accent, what the subject does to the letters, and the one letter it hides. It goes into the image prompt word for word, so write it as an instruction to the model |
| `ui` | Every small text, quoted: wordmark, nav, button, up to three captions |
| `palette` | Three `[name, hex]`: field, second colour (type and quiet surfaces), accent |
| `route` | Leave it out, or `tonal` when the accent is the light itself in the field's colour family (craft.md) |
| `variations` | Five near neighbours of the same page, each changing one thing: the crop (the whole subject, or cut by two edges), the moment (still, or the peak of its movement), the camera (lower or closer), or how far its long part sweeps. `T` below is this skill's folder (`skills/charles-arcade-assets`); run commands from the repo root unless noted. Write

---
name: charles-claude-editing
description: Edit raw talking-head videos into engaging, organic-looking Instagram Reels / TikToks - cut dead space and stumbles, pick the best take, 2-3 word captions, retention-maxing image/video overlays (pop-culture stickers, cutouts, split screens, tweet screenshots), sound effects, a background track from the music folder, and a TikTok-title-style hook when asked. Use this whenever Charles shares a talking-head .MOV/.mp4 and asks to edit, cut, caption, add a hook, add overlays/b-roll/images/a split screen, add music or sound effects, "make it a reel", "minoify" it, or fix any of those in a video already edited this way - even if only one of those steps is asked for.
---

# Goal

* The goal of editing is to maximize viewer retention. The viewer should constantly have something new to look at, without ever feeling overwhelmed
* Keep it organic, like I made it myself on my phone. Use the real thing over a recreation of it: the actual post, footage, app or website, not a mock-up, stock image or AI version. If something looks like a template or AI slop, don't use it
* If something isn't covered here, do whatever best serves those two goals


# Decide these first

```
Is it news (layoffs, announcements, someone else's findings)?
├── Yes → also follow News Videos at the bottom. It wins wherever it disagrees with the defaults
└── No, it's education/entertainment → just the defaults

Did I ask you to open on a split screen?
├── Yes → open on one (see Choosing the Layout)
└── No → open on me
```


# General

* Cut any dead space that exists in the video. Stumbles and false starts count as dead space
* In the case that I filmed multiple takes of the same line, choose the best take
* Safe area (1080x1920): the IG/TikTok header covers the top 250 px, the username and caption sit below y 1500, and the buttons run down the right side below y 840. Keep text at least 80 px from the sides, 140 px below y 840. Be aware of these areas and don't put key information in them, but don't cut off or shift videos and pictures in a weird way because of them. Footage and images can still extend into those areas
* No gimmicks: no pop-ins, rounded corners (except for the hook title), black-background splits or emoji tiles
* My framing is usually close, with my face filling the middle of the frame. In that case never zoom or punch in on my face. Only add slow zooms between cuts when my face is smaller than the middle third of the frame. Cover jump cuts with B-roll instead
* Never isolate or denoise my voice. It struggles to do that well
* If I give you a reference reel, copy its structure, pacing and B-roll, but never its caption style. Captions always follow this file


# Hook Title (the text caption at the top)

* No hook title unless I explicitly ask for one
* When I do: Helvetica Neue Bold near the top of the video, black text on a white background with rounded borders, inside the 80 px side margins. Make it look like TikTok's native text with a background: each line is wrapped individually, so the background bends where a shorter line meets a longer one
* Two lines max. Three is fine when the hook won't fit in two at full size, or when a CAPS word gets its own line
* Usually keep it up for 3-5 s (my first sentence). It can stay longer as long as there's no overlay or B-roll that should replace it


# Captions

* Helvetica Neue Bold, ~66 px, white with a thin black outline and a soft shadow. Sentence case
* Around y 1380, inside the safe area. If an asset sits there, move the captions above or below it, never over it. While a split screen is up, they go on the seam
* 2-3 words each line
* No animations/transitions
* Go over the captions yourself to make sure the ones coming back from a transcription service are accurate to the context of what I'm saying. Sometimes transcription services suffer with names too, so fix those
* Censor any words that tiktok may block the video for, in the captions and the hook (ex: say s*****e instead of suicide)


# Image/Video Overlays

* Use these by default unless I explicitly ask not to
* Make sure every asset is relevant to the video. Don't add assets for the sake of adding assets. Loosely related photos/videos are okay in education/entertainment
* Placement, for overlays that don't take over the whole screen with a blurred background:
   * Where my face sits decides it. If my face is closer to the top, put them below my face and move the captions lower with them. If it's closer to the bottom, put them above my eyes
   * Never cover my eyes or the captions
   * Long screenshots can run off the bottom as long as the highlighted lines stay above y 1500
* Don't blur anything more than it needs, and show assets whole. Don't crop one so part of it gets cut off (ex: the side of a phone screen)
* Never leave black bars around an asset. If it doesn't fill its space (ex: a web page with side margins, a screenshot on a black background), fill the edges with a blur of that same page or asset, or something else related. It's more aesthetic
* You can also place me in front of an image, with an AI cutout of my body in the foreground covering part of it. It adds depth. Only do it when nothing relevant gets covered
* Size images like Instagram stickers rather than full-width slides, so I stay on screen. Tweets, screen recordings and code are the exception, they need to be big enough to read
* If given assets, crop/highlight/adjust them to keep only the relevant parts. Feel free to chop them up to make them more engaging
* If you're finding assets yourself via the web:
   * No stock images. Prioritize images that feel like they were taken by a regular person on their iPhone. Obviously there are exceptions like logos, etc
   * Anchor on pop culture and trends that the viewer would recognize. We want to invoke a familiarity bias
   * Don't create AI generated photographs unless I explicitly ask, because they create an uncanny feeling. Animations and graphics are fine
   * Screenshots of tweets and other social media are great
   * Make sure it's accurate to what I'm talking about (ex: the current Mac mini, not an older model)
* Web pages: dark mode, starting at the visual part, not the intro text. Keep the content inside the 80 px side margins. Light mode pages w/ text running into the screen edge look ugly
* For big claims, show the source (official release, headline) with the words I'm saying highlighted
* Make your own motion graphics and recordings instead of using templates. When I explain a concept, build a visual for it (text, diagrams, graphs, beautiful animations). This is especially potent in educational videos
* When I explain a term, a fix, a technique, a number or a mechanism, ask charles-explainers-assets for the visual at the slot's size, with its text area, my word times and the change words. Place what it returns, and put clicks on its cues
* When you show a list or sequence as a row of pictures, don't use icons. Use organic-looking images you find online, cropped into squares/rectangles
* Graphs and charts are okay. Screenshots of real ones from other sources are great. If you make one yourself, it has to look professional and clean, and be accurate and detailed, w/ well timed animations. A sloppy one comes across as AI slop
* If I read out a list, put it up as an overlay with blur, each item revealed as I say it (plain caption-style text, not a screenshot). If I read it slowly (more than ~4 s between items), take the overlay down between items and bring it back for the next one, so it stays engaging

---

# Goal

Every line I explain gets one visual that a muted viewer understands in the time it's up: the real thing, doing the thing, changing on my word.

**Rich across time, simple within a frame.** Engagement comes from something new happening about every second: a pointer moving in, a state flipping on my word, the fix proving itself, the next asset. Overwhelm comes from things at once. So each frame has one subject and one change, everything else waits its turn or gets cut, and nothing on screen ever sits frozen.

Why: each visual is up for 1-5 s in a card 270-390 pt wide on a phone, next to my face, the list and the captions. My notes have pushed both ways, and the split is space versus time. "Graphics are too busy" (the animation hacks) and "the texts go by too fast" (a comment on design terms) were too much at once. "The video isn't as engaging as I'd like it to be" (unslop repos), "The other deals are too boring when you show them" (Black Friday) and "Stale assets in the screen for too long … should be avoided" (my note on this skill) were too little happening over time. And practice what I teach: my audience learned Hick's law, ease-out and the AI tells from me, so they notice when a visual breaks them.

# The contract

charles-claude-editing usually calls you after picking the layout. You get:
- **The lines:** what I say, the list term, the change word (the word the fix lands on), and word times once the take is cut. Before it's filmed, estimate 4.7 spoken words a second. Count code and numbers as said aloud (100vh is 4 words, 0.95 is 3, 150 is "one fifty", 2), and add 0.2 s at each full stop or question mark. If no change word was given, take the word that names what changes or its cause, and note it.
- **The slot:** its design size, the band the viewer actually sees, the area text must stay inside, and where captions sit. `references/slots.md` has the ones in use.
- **The format:** list reel, hack reel, Day N levels or talking explainer.

You return:
- **One clip per asset** at the slot's design size, rendered at 2× and 60 fps, with no audio. Every line I explain gets at least one asset, and a long line gets more (One asset per item, below).
  - A flip (a before, then an after) is 9.0 s with the change at exactly 4.50 s, the before looping from the start and the after looping to the end. The editor slides it until the change lands on my word and can show any window of it. When my line's before runs past 4.3 s, the hack-reel editor slows the clip's first second to fill the gap, so keep anything whose timing is the lesson out of that second (the push-in and the scene settling are fine).
  - Anything else is the demo's own run from its opening pose, looping where its form loops, with its main move's time in `explain.json` for the editor to retime.
- **`explain.json`:** per line, the takeaway and the change word and time; per asset, its form and a one-line reason, its in and out times, every word shown with its in and out times, and the cursor's actions; and click cues on the clearest changes. That's about four in 45 s at most and never two lines in a row, inside charles-claude-editing's six a minute.
- **`check/phone.png`:** the phone check (below), from `kit/check.mjs`.

Whoever draws the card owns it. In the hack-reel card, the list kit draws the card, its tab and the change from one asset to the next, reading your `explain.json`. Check what the editor draws in any other slot. The UX-principles `assemble.py` only lays clips end to end, so there each clip carries its own card, its tab and, in its first 0.12 s, the fade-through from the previous item's card. In a slot rendered as one span (a Day N card), you draw them too. Never yours: captions, music, sound, the list, title and timer, and where the slot sits. Never burn my spoken words into a clip.

# Workflow

1. **Beat sheet first.** Before building anything, write into `explain.json` for every line: the takeaway in 8 words or fewer, the change word, the subject (the real thing the line is about), and the form of each asset in order. Why: the visual is decided here. A line without a written takeaway gets decoration instead of an explanation.
2. **Pick the form** with the tree below, and give long lines their extra assets.
3. **Fit the frame budget** below.
4. **Build** with the kit (`references/kit.md`): the form from `references/forms.md`, the cursor from `references/agent-cursor.md` and every word on screen from `references/text.md`. Copy the closest gold example named there, or `kit/example/`, and change it; never start from a blank page.
5. **Time it** to my words (Timing, below).
6. **Run the phone check** (`kit/check.mjs` makes the sheet). Fix the largest fault first, re-render, check again.
7. **Hand over** the clips, `explain.json` and the sheet.

# Pick the form

A Day N levels reel skips the tree: every line is a level of the one live demo (`references/forms.md`, Levels). Otherwise walk the tree from the top and take the first branch that fits.

```
What is the line doing?
├── Giving a fix ("Use X", "X looks sloppy, do Y")
│   ├── My line has no problem half (fix-first) → AFTER ONLY: the fix in action, tagged After
│   ├── The flaw shows in a still frame (radius, contrast, alignment, spacing, copy)
│   │   └── FLIP IN PLACE: one crop, the flaw, then the fix on the change word
│   └── The flaw is motion or timing (duration, easing, stagger, jank, spring)
│       ├── The versions differ only in feel (the same duration on another curve, a spring
│       │   against a tween, durations under 2× apart), on a simple element whose moving
│       │   part stays 40 px or bigger at half width, in a slot that doesn't tag its clips
│       │   Before/After (the hack-reel card does)
│       │   └── SIDE BY SIDE: both start on the same frame, labelled only with their values
│       └── Otherwise (600 ms against 200 ms, a pop out of nothing) → FLIP IN PLACE
├── Naming a principle or a law: a rule that one way works better than another
│   ("Anticipation wind-up", "Hick's law", "Snappy timing", "Frequency of use")
│   ├── The slot tags its clips Before/After and flips the tag (the hack-reel card)
│   │   └── FLIP IN PLACE, the change on the principle's name
│   ├── Its "without" version isn't a mistake anyone makes: it names a way of working,
│   │   not a better result (pose to pose)
│   │   └── DEMO + DEFINITION TAB
│   └── Otherwise → SIDE BY SIDE: the same component without the principle (left, Before)
│       and with it (right, After), running from the same frame, under the definition tab
├── Naming a term the viewer may not know: what a thing is called ("Kerning", "OKLCH", "Tabular numbers")
│   └── DEMO + DEFINITION TAB: one move that shows the term, with no Before/After; the tab
│       says what it means. A word most of my viewers already know gets the move alone

Use when a screen or component works but feels off or unfinished, when asked to polish, refine, take it further, or make it feel great, when adding or reviewing animation, or when reviewing UI against a high craft bar. If the screen still looks AI-generated, run charles-unslop first."
---

# Polish

Built from Emil Kowalski's UI polish and animation skills, Josh Puckett's Interface Craft, and feedback from Charles Liu's "Removing AI Slop" series.

Most work stops at level 3 of 10, because it works and it's easy to stop. The difference between fine and great is rarely the idea; it's how far the idea gets pushed. Most "something feels off" problems are one wrong note, so look, measure and name it before changing anything.

## Run it

1. **Render it,** at its real size and at the smallest size it will be seen. Capture each state and each motion as frames. Measure in the pixels people see: on a scaled stage, a 42 px button may be 37 px on screen.
2. **Score it** against the anchors below and name the weakest thing on screen in one sentence.
3. **Structure:** fix hierarchy and containers before details. Polishing the wrong structure is wasted work.
4. **States:** map every state, including empty, loading, error and success, and design the unhappy ones.
5. **Details:** run the details table.
6. **Motion:** walk the three decision trees, then storyboard.
7. **Verify** frame by frame (below). Nothing is done until you've looked at the frames.
8. **Climb:** run the loop until two passes in a row find nothing that changes the score.

If you were asked to review and not to change anything, stop before step 8 and report each finding as severity, what's wrong, the evidence (frame, number or file and line) and the fix. High means a state is broken or a promise the screen makes isn't kept. Medium means people notice. Low means only a designer does.

### Score anchors

| Score | It means |
| --- | --- |
| 3 | It works, and looks like everything else |
| 5 | Designed at rest, but unhappy states or motion are default |
| 7 | Every state is designed and motion is correct; nothing is memorable yet |
| 8 | One thing people would screenshot, no visible defect at the viewing size |
| 9 | That thing holds up in every state and input path, and a rival would copy it |
| 10 | Don't award this to your own work |

## The climb

Think in levels. Early levels fix what's broken, and you can see what to do. Later levels are invention, and you can't, so use a move:

| Stuck because | Move |
| --- | --- |
| You don't know what better is | **Zoom in.** Take one element at 3×. What if this were the only thing on screen? |
| It's busy | **Remove something.** Did you actually need it? |
| It feels off | **Name it** in one sentence, even before you know the fix |
| It's fine but plain | **Reference the best.** Find the world-class version and list what it does that yours doesn't |
| You keep tweaking one idea | **Generate more.** Make three genuinely different versions, compare at real size, keep one |
| You can't see it anymore | **Critique.** Get a fresh reader with no context, or re-read your own work as a rival would |

Rules for climbing:

- **Each level is one nameable move with a reason.** "Add a spring" isn't a reason; "it can be redirected mid-flight, so it never blocks you" is. If you can't say why in a sentence, the change isn't honest.
- **Make the first leap the biggest.** Going from default to designed must be obvious in a still. If before and after look alike, the default wasn't default enough or the change wasn't structural.
- **Each level is strictly better than the last.** Never ship a deliberately broken step; a demonstrated bug looks like a bug.
- **Name the thing people would screenshot.** If there isn't one, that's the next job.
- **Push the concept into the material,** not effects on top of it. If the idea is a pressure gauge, the needle is the loading state, not a spinner beside it.
- **Undo your own decisions** when they stop holding up. Restraint counts as a level.
- **Land success as the peak.** The end of a flow is what people remember. If success is only a label swap, push the concept into it: the thing the screen has been holding back happens now.
- **Every input path reaches the same ending.** Pointer, keyboard, a slow gesture and reduced motion may travel differently, but all of them end with the same state and the same best detail.

## Details

Absence is what gets noticed, so run all of these. If you're short on time, start with form behavior, hit area, contrast and layout shift, because those are the ones people feel. Express them in the project's own styling system.

| Check | Rule | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fonts | `-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased`; subset files | Crisper text, nothing unused shipped |
| Field and button | A resting button and a field never share one fill. The field stays the brightest; a waiting button sits one tone down | Two identical white slabs hide which one you type in |
| Cast light | Window shadows and light patterns stop at an object's edge | Bars running unbroken from the table across paper read as seeing through the paper |
| Dynamic numbers | `tabular-nums` | Digits that change width make neighbors jiggle |
| Weight | Never change `font-weight` on hover or selection; use color | It reflows text |
| Layout shift | Fixed dimensions or `aspect-ratio` for skeletons, images, async content; reserve space for messages | Jumping content reads as broken |
| Typography | `…` `’` `“ ”`; `text-wrap: balance` on headings, `pretty` on body; 45–75ch measure; body leading 1.4–1.6, display ~1.1 | Punctuation and rag are where care shows |
| Tracking | Caps at any size +0.08em. Other text: none below 28px, −0.01em at 28–47px, −0.022em from 48px | Large type wants tighter, caps want air |
| Sizes | At most 5 type sizes, one vertical grid | Fewer things |
| Alignment | At most 2–3 dominant vertical lines; icons on a center spine, text on a left edge | Stray lines are what "off" usually is |
| Optical | Icon side of a button −2 to −3 px padding; play triangles 2 px toward the point; fix asymmetric icons in the SVG | Equal numbers often look unequal, so eyes win |
| Radius | Inner = outer − padding; one radius family | Mismatched nesting is visible |
| Borders | Transparent rings: `box-shadow: 0 0 0 1px rgb(0 0 0/.08)` | They adapt to any surface |
| Style | One icon style, one material, one neutral temperature | The odd one out reads as a bug |
| Color fit | Success and error marks are hues from the page's palette, or adjusted toward it. Real-world meanings stay (a delayed flight may be amber) | A stock green check on an ink page reads as borrowed |
| Contrast | Body and labels ≥4.5:1, large text and icons ≥3:1, measured over the real background. Nothing people must read under 12 px at the viewing size | "Legible" isn't a judgment call |
| Press | `scale(0.96)`, never below 0.95 | Tactile without exaggeration |
| Hover | Named properties, ~150ms; gate to `(hover: hover)`; no layout change | `transition: all` animates things you didn't choose |
| Focus | Keep it; neutral color only | Brand-colored rings clash |
| Hit area | ≥44×44 touch, ≥40×40 desktop, via a pseudo-element; never overlapping; make whole surfaces the target | Small targets miss (Fitts's law) |
| Stacking | `isolation: isolate` or a fixed z-index scale | `9999` means nobody knows |
| Decoration | `pointer-events: none`, `user-select: none` | It can't steal clicks |
| First paint | Resolve state before render: never defa

skills.excerpt:
---
name: charles-storage-cleanup
description: Investigate Mac disk usage, find rarely used apps and overlooked storage, and clean authorized disposable caches, runtimes, devices, research artifacts, and development files while preserving active work.
---

# Storage Cleanup

Recover space from confirmed disposable artifacts, explain recent growth, and preserve active work. Measure success with free bytes on the actual data volume.

## Scope and authorization

When the request authorizes removing unused files, delete confirmed disposable candidates without repeated confirmation. An inventory-only request stays read-only. Skill discovery alone grants no deletion permission. Carry forward the user's selected items, exclusions, age limits, and recent-use conditions across passes; a request to inspect more locations does not revoke a previous keep instruction.

Keep active apps, builds, Git writers, and emulators running. Do not cancel a job to turn its files into deletion candidates. Preserve source, uncommitted work, credentials, unique research/media, current releases, and persistent VM/container data unless their removal is explicitly authorized. A generic request to clear unused files does not supply that authorization. An old modification time, ignored Git status, or absent open handle alone does not establish disposability. Skip uncertain candidates and continue useful cleanup elsewhere.

## Choose the depth

- For a named deletion, inspect that selection and its dependencies, then complete the authorized cleanup. A whole-app uninstall includes its own helpers and startup registrations; cache-only cleanup does not.
- For general cleanup, unused-app reviews, "what else," or "search more extensively," use [the discovery checklist](references/discovery.md). Cover installed software, both Library trees, hidden package stores, runtimes, developer/research output, devices, media/downloads, and OS-managed storage. Do not stop at the largest project or `~/Library/Caches`.
- When explaining a large folder, break it into source, generated output, installed environments, Git history, and unique assets. Describe what the largest payloads actually contain and why they exist before recommending removal.

## Workflow

1. **Baseline and map the machine.** Record local time, data-volume free bytes, recent cleanup receipts, mounts, and active work. Store audits privately outside repositories, under `~/Library/Logs/storage-cleanup/`. Start with filesystem-bounded directory sizes, including hidden directories and shared/system application data; deepen large branches with bounded probes.
2. **Cover overlooked families.** In a broad audit, work through the discovery checklist and record each family as measured, absent, excluded, or not fully inspected. Follow configured cache/SDK locations and sibling or agent workspaces. Revisit newly exposed smaller contributors after large removals. Previously deleted paths and old measurements are not new opportunities.
3. **Establish disposability and inactivity.** Identify reconstruction inputs, an obsolete duplicate, or a documented cache purpose. Distinguish the eligible subset from an entire installation or cache pool. Independently inspect relevant processes, arguments/cwd, open files, and running devices. Refresh checks before deletion. A failed or truncated usage probe leaves use unknown. Missing app-use metadata means unknown use.
4. **Remove in measured batches.** Log exact paths, sizes, reasons, reconstruction metadata, and methods. Prefer supported SDK/device/package-manager commands. For direct removal, validate the specific path, avoid symlink targets, and preserve nonstandard data or local patches. Do not use blanket repository cleaning. Finish all eligible user-level work and prepare one reviewable exact batch before requesting necessary administrator authentication; verify the child job's result rather than only the authorization helper's exit status.
5. **Investigate recurrence.** If free space falls again, compare observations and trace writers. Repeated abandoned Git packs warrant checking background `git add` and generated payloads. Use a backed-up, scoped machine-local exclusion only for confirmed generated material; verify tracked files and useful new reports/scripts remain visible. Do not blindly copy another project's ignore patterns.
6. **Verify and report.** Check removed paths, retained active resources, unchanged dependency lockfiles, and readable Git commits where relevant. After runtime removal, verify retained dependent environments and the default executable. After an uninstall, check the app, its selected remnants, and its own services. Report current free space, measured recovery, concurrent growth, reinstall requirements, unresolved items, and coverage gaps. Folder allocations and deletion totals are not physical recovery estimates.

For an opportunity list, give stable numbers, exact paths or selectors, measured eligible sizes, contents/purpose, use evidence, and the condition for safe removal. Separate regenerable caches, optional installed software, and data needing a user decision. Do not inflate savings with overlapping parents/children, all versions when one must remain, empty device registrations, sparse-disk maximum capacity, or personal artifacts labeled as cache. If fewer than the requested number of useful verified candidates remain, report that and the uninspected areas instead of padding the list.

| Candidate | Evidence needed in addition to inactivity |
| --- | --- |
| Dependencies/builds | Known generated installation/output; retained lockfiles, build inputs, or environment metadata; no tracked/custom content lost |
| APK/IPA/installers | Obsolete or redundant artifact; retain current release/reviewer builds and any unique analysis evidence |
| Emulators/simulators | Known disposable QA device with no current task/data dependency; shutdown alone is insufficient |
| Git temporary packs | Git garbage classification, stable separate observations, no live writer/handle, valid history preserved |
| Model/package caches | Re-downloadable contents; preserve authentication, installed environments, active models, and persistent data |
| Rarely used apps/extensions | Bundle or extension identity, measured payload, current activity, and recorded last use or an explicit unknown; retained user data and shared components |
| Old/duplicate runtimes | Architecture, version, default selection, executable links, dependent environments, and embedded app runtimes; pool size is not all removable |
| Downloads/history/logs | The user's exact age and recent-use criteria, supported record timestamps where applicable, and no unique required content or live writer |

## Tools and conditional details

Use [the discovery checklist](references/discovery.md) for broad audits. Read the relevant sections of [macOS cleanup notes](references/macos.md) before app/runtime uninstalls, privileged cleanup, Git objects, devices/SDKs, or compression. They also cover activity probes, APFS sharing, and virtual DeviceFS accounting.

The bundled helper inventories **metadata only**; it never decides what to delete or removes files. It skips symlinks and child filesystems, deduplicates hardlinks per root, and compares earlier snapshots. Paths below assume the default personal skill location; resolve relative to this skill if installed elsewhere.

```bash
cleanup_audit="$HOME/Library/Logs/storage-cleanup/$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
umask 077
mkdir -p "$cleanup_audit"
python3 "<this skill's folder>/scripts/inventory.py" \
  --root "$HOME/Developer" --output "$cleanup_audit/inventory.json"
```

Use `--help` for additional roots, output limits, and `--compare`. `--max-depth` limits directory summaries, not traversal: scan selected roots progressively and bound expensive probes. Broad scans can take time; keep the user updated and inspect compact summaries rather than dumping inventories. A partial scan must remain labeled partial.

---

# Store screenshots

A screenshot set is one strip of frames designed as one picture. Frames 1–2 are the hook: one composition that makes people want the rest. Every seam is crossed, so the set feels like a single world you scroll through, and each later frame shows one real moment of the app. Sets are built in HTML, so type and real UI stay crisp, with generated objects and real photos composited in, and rendered to Apple's exact size.

Before planning, read [references/craft.md](references/craft.md): the lane tree, hook techniques, seam recipes, type, copy and the tells. For reference sets, read [references/swipe.md](references/swipe.md).

## The bar

Every set passes all nine. Each exists because breaking it made sets look templated, generated or unreadable.

1. **Frames 1–2 are one hook.** One photo, scene, object, headline or sentence crosses the seam between them, and together they say what the app is and why it's worth it. Frame 1 alone still shows the app's name or face and its promise. Why: the opening spread is what nearly everyone sees. One image across it reads as a poster, and the half that continues pulls the swipe. Ads and some search layouts show frame 1 alone, so it can't lean on frame 2.
2. **Every seam is crossed.** Each seam is crossed by a continuous background, or by an object, person, phone or type reaching 24 px or more into the next frame (72 px in the export). At least half the seams are crossed by a distinct shape (an object, a person, a phone, type, a drawn line or a shaft of light), not only by a flat ground. Alternating frame colours are fine when something crosses the colour change. Why: continuity makes the set one world. A row of separate cards reads as a template.
3. **One idea per frame after the hook, six words or fewer.** One headline of at most six words, plus an optional eyebrow of at most four. In the chaotic lane, one lead line obeys this; bubbles and stickers are texture and must read as part of the picture, never as a second headline. Why: Hick's law. # Unreasonable Craft

Go above and beyond with the design. Don't settle for the first idea, or for what you think counts as "good" design. That's AI slop. Push past what you think is creatively possible. Hold an uncommon, excessively high bar for craft and attention to detail, with unreasonable standards. Violating the letter of this skill is violating its spirit.

**The bar:** good enough to win Site of the Day on awwwards.com (for websites) *and* an Apple Design Award (for apps). It really needs to be that good. Anything less falls short, and you say so.

Paths here are relative to this skill's folder. The scripts need Node 18+, ffmpeg, and Google Chrome; their packages are in `scripts/node_modules` (if that's missing, run `npm install --prefix <this skill's folder>/scripts`).

- When they fit: `apple-design` (physical, interruptible motion and materials), `animate` / `animate-expo` (building motion), `emil-design-eng` (component polish). They sit next to this skill (`../<name>/SKILL.md`).

## Design from a system

Everything you make should come from one coherent system, and you should stay faithful to it. To find that system, in order:

1. **The project's design system** (tokens, theme, components, style guide), if there is one.
2. **Otherwise, the project's existing UI.** Reuse what's already there so the new work feels like it always belonged.
3. **Otherwise (a new project), one you invent.** Build a rough system from the chosen direction (color tokens, type, spacing, radii, elevation, motion, a few core components), write it down as tokens, and design from it.

Be bold *within* the system. Fill gaps in its own language, propose changes instead of drifting silently, and treat anything off-system as a bug.

## Track it

Copy this checklist into your plan or todo list and tick it off as you go. The work isn't done while a box is open.

```
- [ ] Explore: 3+ directions rendered side by side; one picked, with reasons
- [ ] System: found, inferred, or invented, and written down as tokens
- [ ] Assets: generated with today's best models, art-directed, optimized
- [ ] Polish: every value on purpose, copy in the user's voice, every screen size
- [ ] Verify: captured, measured, and read frame by frame
- [ ] Critique: one round by a fresh critic (more only if the user asked), fixes verified
- [ ] Final pass: zero mistakes
```

Keep a design log in the project: the direction and why, the system, every critique round's scores and fixes, and open issues. Use the project's own place for design reviews if it has one (such as `docs/reviews/`); otherwise create `docs/design/<topic>-<date>/`. Long sessions get summarized, and the log is how you keep your place: after a summary or a restart, reread this file and the log before going on.

- Concept and narrative: what feeling or metaphor holds the whole thing together?
- Layout and composition, grid, rhythm, negative space
- Typography: faces, scale, leading, tracking, numerals
- Color: palette, neutrals, contrast, light/dark behavior

# Unslop

Adapted from [unslop](https://github.com/heydamir/unslop) by Damir Sokolovsky ([@heydamir](https://x.com/heydamir)), CC BY 4.0, merged with Emil Kowalski's unslop-design skill and with feedback from Charles Liu's "Removing AI Slop" series. Changes: the passes were reordered around subtraction, and the rules on backgrounds, brand icons and materials were rewritten. Keep this credit in copies.

Nobody can point at the one element that makes a screen look generated. A model picks the most common option for every decision at once, and fifty median choices compound into a watermark. So fixing one element does nothing: walk the whole screen, in order.

Removing the tells is half the job. A clean screen that could belong to any product is the next template. Slop spreads richness over the chrome; craft keeps the chrome quiet and spends it on one moment.

## Run it

1. **Render it.** Screenshot the screen at its real size and judge that, not the code. If it will be seen small (a phone, a video, a thumbnail), judge it at that size too.
2. **Audit.** Walk [references/signs.md](references/signs.md). List every sign, one line each, with where it lives.
3. **Choose the scope** from the audit:

   - A designed screen with a few signs → fix only those. Keep its palette, type, layout and visual. Put bigger ideas in the report.
   - No signs → say so, suggest at most three refinements with exact values, and stop. Never change a good screen to make it different.
4. **Write the direction** (below). Show the audit and direction and wait for an answer, because a wrong direction redoes everything. Skip the wait only if told to just do it.
5. **Subtract.**
6. **Run the passes in order,** finishing each across the whole screen.
7. **Run the final audit.** Anything that fails goes back to its pass.

Keep the product. Features, real content and section order stay, and the product keeps its name. Never invent capabilities, or claims and facts about a real product; a new way of presenting something the product already does is design, not an invented feature. Placeholder content in a demo or mock may be replaced with specifics. Filler like "Powered by AI" or "Follow us for deals" isn't a feature, so it can go.

## Direction

Five lines, derived from what the product does, never from what's trending.

- **Product:** what it does and for whom, in one sentence.
- **Character:** two or three concrete words, like `calm, exact, a little warm`. Clean, modern, sleek, minimal and premium are banned because they describe every template.
- **World:** the place or material the product belongs to. A tide-table app lives near salt, charts and low light; a tax tool near ruled ledgers. The world sets the neutral tint and the accent. It doesn't have to become a picture.
- **Moment:** the one or two places the screen gets its richness. See pass 8: it may be a behaviour, real content, proportion, type or an object.
- **Signature:** one small detail only this product would have, used consistently.

Then write the **concept**: one sentence every later choice can be checked against. Example: "Every invoice reads like a letter from one person to another." Two checks before you keep it:

- **Does it survive the next state?** Walk it through empty, in use and done. A concept that only works on the opening frame is a poster, not a concept.
- **Did you write it to justify something you already wanted?** Then it filters nothing. It must rule out at least one thing you'd otherwise do.

**If the screen names no product,** ask. If you can't ask, or were told to just do it, then:

- A mock or demo: assume one specific, plausible product and write the whole direction for it, with `Product (assumed):` so it can be overruled. Never use a stray word in the copy as the world, and don't default to SaaS. Assume something with a particular world, since that's what gives the palette, type and accent something to come from. It must fit the features you're keeping: a GitHub button rules out a bakery. The world needn't become an object on screen. White, black and a system font with no reason is a template too.
- A real product you don't know: keep it neutral, make no claims, and list what you'd need to know.

Keep a real brand mark or color. A violet-to-blue gradient, a sparkle tile or a glossy orb doesn't count as brand unless the user says so.

## Subtract first

Agents add. A caption restating the heading, an icon on every label, a divider spacing already provides, a border on a surface with a shadow, a second CTA, a helper line under the input. Each is defensible and together they compete.

Walk every icon, line, badge, caption, container and word and ask: **what breaks if this is gone?** "Nothing" means delete. "It adds interest" and "it fills space" are why the model put it there, so they don't count. Walk twice, because deletions expose each other. The one signature from the direction is exempt, and only that one. If an element carries information people need (a password's rules, a price), move it, shrink it, or make it the moment; don't lose it.

The cuts generated screens need most:

- **Dividers.** Delete every divider that spacing can replace; proximity already groups things, and lines add noise. Lists, settings rows and suggestion chips almost never need them. Lines in a ledger or a table that help the eye track across a row can stay.
- **Subtitles under titles.** Delete unless they say something the title can't.
- **Nesting.** A container inside a container inside a card is a tell. If a map, image or chart is the content, run it to the edges of its parent. Delete wrappers until each surface has a job.
- **Two mechanisms for one job.** A progress bar and a step counter, a toast and a visible change, an icon and a label saying the same thing. Keep the better one. This isn't cutting a feature: the job still gets done.
- **Bolted-on controls.** A button floating beside a field belongs inside the field, as part of its empty or focused state.
- **Chrome the moment doesn't need,** like a Share button on something with nothing to share yet.

The order matters: rhythm changes how everything else reads, and copy length decides type size and layout. Visuals and motion come last so they fit a screen that already works without them. Exact starting values are in [references/tokens.md](references/tokens.md).

# UX & Animation

From Charles Liu's "20 Principles of UX & Animation" reel, extended with Emil Kowalski's rules for interface animation, the motion techniques in Josh Puckett's Interface Craft, and more of the laws of UX. Built on Disney's 12 principles of animation (Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, *The Illusion of Life*), Raphael Salaja's userinterface.wiki and Jon Yablonski's Laws of UX.

Every interaction answers five questions, in this order: should it move, where should the eye go, how should it move, can people find it, hit it and choose it, and can they finish. Walk them in that order every time. A later answer never rescues an earlier one: the perfect curve on an animation that shouldn't exist is still wrong.

## Run it

1. **Match the stack.** Find what the project already animates with (CSS transitions, Tailwind, Motion as `motion` or `framer-motion`, React Spring, WAAPI) and write in that. State changes stay in CSS transitions. If Motion is installed, use it only for what CSS can't do: animating an element out as it unmounts, layout changes, and springs that follow a finger. Never add a library for what a CSS transition does, and never hand-roll a spring where Motion is installed. Why: two systems animating the same kind of change drift apart in timing and in how they handle interruption.
2. **List the interactions** in scope. For each, write down what triggers it (pointer, touch, keyboard, network, scroll), how often one person fires it, and what it has to tell them. Then cut, or in a review flag, every element and step that doesn't serve the task (Occam's razor, question 5) before polishing anything. Why: restyling something that's about to be deleted is wasted work.
3. **Walk questions 1–5** below, question by question, checking every interaction against each rule. Each subsection says when it applies; skip it when nothing in scope can trigger it (if nothing travels across the screen, skip Arcs).
4. **Name the numbers.** Durations, curves and springs live in named tokens at the top of the file or in the theme, and every animation uses them. A sequence of three or more stages gets a storyboard: a comment listing when each stage starts, a `TIMING` object, and one config object per element ([storyboards](references/techniques.md#storyboards)). When you can run the app, tune the values live (a dev-only control panel), then hard-code what works. Why: a number nobody can find is a number nobody tunes.
5. **Verify** with the checks at the end.

Recipes with exact values for modals, drawers, popovers, tooltips, toasts, entrances, exits, expanders, icon swaps, async buttons, numbers, sliders and carousels are in [references/recipes.md](references/recipes.md), with code wherever a value isn't enough. Curves, springs, interruptibility, arcs, mapping one value to another, rubber banding, loops, masks, cross-fades, storyboards, timelines and performance are in [references/techniques.md](references/techniques.md). Both files open with a list of their sections; read the section a rule points to.

**Reviewing instead of building?** Open the report with the interaction list from step 2. Then write one table row per finding: severity, principle, where (file and line, or frame), before, after. Severity is **broken** (a wrong result, lost input, a blocked or skipped step), **friction** (slower or more confusing than it needs to be) or **polish**. Sort by severity, then by the five questions; a Verify finding goes under the question it serves (reduced motion and animated properties under 3). Bugs no principle covers go in a list after the table.

## 1. Should it move?

### Frequency of use

```
How often will one person trigger this?
├── Many times a session, or from the keyboard (shortcuts, arrow keys, ⌘K, tabs, focus moving)
│     → no transition. The new state shows on the next frame.
├── A few times a session (menu, popover, modal, drawer, toast, saving a form)
│     → animate, within the timing table in question 3.
└── Rarely: a milestone the person won't repeat this session (onboarding, a first success, finishing a big task)
      → may be choreographed: each move up to 500ms, the whole sequence up to about 2.5s.

Then: does the motion answer a question? (Where did this come from? Did my action register? What changed? What caused it?)
├── No  → cut it.
└── Yes → keep it, and make the motion say the answer (question 3, "Make it mean something").
```

Press and hover feedback is exempt: it keeps its 100–150ms transition at every frequency, because it's the response itself. When hover and a keyboard highlight share a style, put the transition on the hover rule only, so the keys stay instant. Marketing pages can run longer and showier; product UI stays inside the timing table. Why: the hundredth time someone sees an animation, it stops informing and starts delaying. Keyboard users act faster than any transition, so a highlight that glides falls behind the keys.

Nothing that is already at rest when the page first paints plays an entrance: motion is for the changes people cause afterward. In Motion, set `initial={false}` on `AnimatePresence` around toggles, tabs and icon swaps, and never around a first-run entrance whose whole point is to play.

### Doherty threshold

People stay in flow when the interface answers within 400ms.

- The pressed state shows on the same frame as the input, never after a network round trip.
- Update optimistically when an action almost never fails: like, favorite, toggle, reorder, mark as read, send a message, remove an item. The change starts on the same frame (a motion that starts at once counts), and rolls back with a message if the server refuses.
- In a multi-step flow, a step that passes validation in the browser saves in the background while people move on, and a failed save shows a toast with Retry that keeps their new place. The exception is a step whose result the next one needs (shipping and tax depend on the saved address): it waits like a final submit.
- Everything else, including every final submit (paying, placing an order): disable the trigger at once against double submits, and show "Saving…" or a spinner only after 300ms, held at least 500ms once shown ([async buttons](references/recipes.md#async-buttons)). 给出时长表与退出比进入短20–30%等具体数值规则
要求时长、曲线、弹簧写成命名 token，三段以上序列用 storyboard
审查时输出交互清单与按严重度排序的表格：severity、principle、where、before、after
引用 recipes.md 与 techniques.md 获取模态、抽屉、弹出层等配方与曲线、弹簧、性能细节
inputs: 项目现有动画技术栈（CSS transitions、Tailwind、Motion、React Spring、WAAPI）
范围内交互清单：触发方式、单人触发频率、需传达的信息
待审查的界面代码或帧（文件行号或帧号）
outputs: 按五问顺序的构建或审查结论
审查报告：开头为交互清单，随后每行一条发现（严重度、原则、位置、改前、改后），按严重度与五问排序
命名 token 与 storyboard 形式的时长、曲线、弹簧配置
scenarios: 新增或审查动画、过渡、手势与微交互
设计加载态、乐观更新与异步按钮反馈
审查菜单、弹出层、模态、抽屉、Toast 等组件动效
审查表单、引导与多步流程的反馈与节奏
检查 reduced motion 与动画性能问题
prerequisites: 项目已有动画技术栈，需先确认并沿用
若已安装 Motion，仅用于 CSS 做不到的场景
可运行应用时可用仅开发环境的控制面板实时调参
limits: 仅依据原文，未说明具体宿主平台与安装方式
营销页可更长更炫，产品 UI 须守在时长表内
按压与悬停反馈在任何频率下都保留 100–150ms 过渡
错误抖动等夸张手法仅用于必须被感知的时刻
已处于静止状态的元素在首帧不播放入场动画

evidence.quote: Every interaction answers five questions, in this order: should it move, where should the eye go, how should it move, can people find it, hit it and choose it, and can they finish.
Durations, curves and springs live in named tokens at the top of the file or in the theme, and every animation uses them.
A sequence of three or more stages gets a storyboard: a comment listing when each stage starts, a `TIMING` object, and one config object per element
Then write one table row per finding: severity, principle, where (file and line, or frame), before, after.
Recipes with exact values for modals, drawers, popovers, tooltips, toasts, entrances, exits, expanders, icon swaps, async buttons, numbers, sliders and carousels are in [references/recipes.md]
Find what the project already animates with (CSS transitions, Tailwind, Motion as `motion` or `framer-motion`, React Spring, WAAPI) and write in that.
If Motion is installed, use it only for what CSS can't do: animating an element out as it unmounts, layout changes, and springs that follow a finger.
When you can run the app, tune the values live (a dev-only control panel), then hard-code what works.
Marketing pages can run longer and showier; product UI stays inside the timing table.
Press and hover feedback is exempt: it keeps its 100–150ms transition at every frequency, because it's the response itself.
Nothing that is already at rest when the page first paints plays an entrance: motion is for the changes people cause afterward.
Use when adding or reviewing animation, transitions, gestures, micro-interactions, loading and optimistic states, feedback, targets, menus, forms, onboarding or multi-step flows.
Open the report with the interaction list from step 2.
Severity is **broken** (a wrong result, lost input, a blocked or skipped step), **friction** (slower or more confusing than it needs to be) or **polish**.
